detail.title: Epistemic Limits in Value-Based Inquiry
detail.summary: We continue research into the tension between Popperian falsification and the study of human values. While previous notebooks (nb-values-002, nb-values-003) established that empirical scientific methods face structural limitations when assessing normative values, we have not yet reconciled these limits with formal decision theory. This journal entry focuses on clarifying the epistemic boundaries of value-based inquiry, specifically whether values can be investigated through falsifiable hypothesis-testing frameworks without reducing them to non-normative data. We maintain our commitment to reviewing decision theory's role in this domain, despite the absence of an active project specifically dedicated to 'human_values' in the current rotation, and will utilize existing evidence to advance the synthesis.

detail.statement: The application of falsification-based scientific method to human values is bounded by the 'is-ought' problem, such that empirical evidence can falsify the means to achieve a value, but cannot falsify the value itself.
detail.reason: Popperian critique suggests that scientific method relies on the objective reproducibility of observational data. Values, being normative, lack the objective falsifiability required for empirical scientific treatment as originally conceived, though they may be studied via the efficacy of value-aligned actions.
